sections.title: 9.1 ML-KEM Implementation
sections.summary: How an ML-KEM key is laid out, why the 64-byte seed is the real private key, and how to check every field of a decapsulation key.

blocks.markdown:
FIPS 203 specifies ML-KEM as three algorithms (KeyGen, Encaps, Decaps) built on an internal public-key scheme K-PKE, and it is strict about how they may be used. K-PKE **must not** be used as a stand-alone encryption scheme; only the three ML-KEM algorithms are approved, and the internal deterministic functions (KeyGen_internal, Encaps_internal, Decaps_internal) **should not be exposed to applications** other than for testing, because the randomness has to be generated inside the cryptographic module (FIPS 203, section 3.3). A conforming implementation may replace the specified steps by any mathematically equivalent procedure, so the standard fixes *behaviour*, not code structure.

The key formats are fixed. The encapsulation key is ek = (k polynomials in 384·k bytes) ‖ ρ (32 bytes); the decapsulation key is dk = dk_PKE (384·k bytes) ‖ ek ‖ H(ek) (32 bytes) ‖ z (32 bytes), where ρ comes from G(d ‖ k), H is SHA3-256 and z is a secret value used for rejection (section 7.1). Key generation draws two 32-byte strings d and z, and the pair (d, z) determines every other byte. The listing checks all of this on the three parameter sets: the key derived from a seed is reproducible, ek ends with ρ = G(d ‖ k), dk has the stated four-part layout, H(ek) is the SHA3-256 of the embedded ek, and z is the second half of the seed. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

blocks.markdown:
Every structural property holds for ML-KEM-512, -768 and -1024. The practical consequence is that a **64-byte seed is the complete private key**: the whole decapsulation key (1,632 to 3,168 bytes) can be regenerated from it, which makes backup, audit and recovery simpler, and storing only the seed is the format modern key-management interfaces prefer (the OpenSSL-based API used in 9.11 exposes keys exactly this way). The trade-off is that regenerating the key costs a key generation each time it is needed, and the seed must then be protected exactly like the key.

**Common mistakes:** exposing a function that takes the randomness as a parameter (it makes the secret-dependent value controllable by a caller; keep it for known-answer tests only), reusing d or z across keys, and confusing the roles of the two seed halves: d determines the lattice keys, while z only affects what is returned for invalid ciphertexts (9.5).

sections.title: 9.2 ML-DSA Implementation
sections.summary: ML-DSA key and signature structure, deterministic versus hedged signing, context strings and signature rejection, all verified.

blocks.markdown:
ML-DSA (FIPS 204) is a lattice signature in the Fiat-Shamir-with-aborts style. A public key is ρ (32 bytes, the seed of the public matrix) followed by the packed high bits t1 of the key vector; a private key starts with ρ, a 32-byte secret K and tr = SHAKE256(pk, 64 bytes), followed by the packed secret vectors. Signing computes a message representative from tr, the context and the message, and then repeats a **rejection-sampling loop** until the candidate signature does not leak information about the secret; the number of rounds varies from one signature to the next, which affects timing but not security when done correctly (see C10). The standard offers a **deterministic** variant (all randomness derived from the key and message) and a **hedged** variant that mixes in 32 fresh random bytes, and the hedged one is the default because it also protects against some fault attacks (FIPS 204; the choice between them is part of the signing interface).

Signatures can carry a **context string** of at most 255 bytes that is bound into the signed data, so a signature made for one purpose cannot be replayed for another. The listing verifies the key structure for all three sets and the relation tr = SHAKE256(pk, 64), shows that deterministic signing repeats while hedged signing does not, that every signature verifies, and tests context binding and single-bit corruption. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

blocks.markdown:
For all three sets pk begins with ρ, the private key stores ρ in its first 32 bytes and tr = SHAKE256(pk) at offset 64, and the public key can be recomputed from the private key. Deterministic signing returns the identical signature each time, hedged signing never repeats, and all four verify. The context behaves as intended: a signature for the context "firmware-update" verifies only under that context; a context of 256 bytes is rejected at signing time; and corrupting any one of 301 sampled bit positions of the 3,309-byte signature makes verification fail.

**Engineering points.** (1) Use a different context string for each protocol or purpose; that costs nothing and removes cross-protocol replay. (2) Prefer the hedged variant unless a deterministic signature is a requirement (for example for reproducible test vectors), and never mix the two in one deployment without a reason. (3) The rejection loop makes signing time variable by design; the variability must not depend on secret data beyond what the algorithm's proof allows.

sections.title: 9.3 SLH-DSA Implementation
sections.summary: A toy stateful hash-based signer showing the structure of such code (WOTS chains, Merkle tree, index state) and why state handling is the main engineering risk, plus estimated hash-call counts for the FIPS 205 sets.

blocks.markdown:
SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) is **stateless**: a signer does not have to remember which one-time keys it has used, because it signs with a pseudo-randomly chosen leaf of a very large hypertree and a few-time FORS signature at the bottom. Its implementation is dominated by **hash calls**: the signer recomputes whole XMSS subtrees (which makes signing slow, especially for the "s" parameter sets) while the verifier recomputes only the chain tails and authentication paths (which makes verification fast). There is no big-number or polynomial arithmetic at all, which makes the code small and the security argument simple, and implementations differ mostly in how they parallelise and batch the hash function.

There is no SLH-DSA implementation available in this lab, so the listing builds a **toy stateful** scheme (the structure of XMSS: WOTS chains with a checksum, a Merkle tree of 16 one-time keys, a counter that must be advanced before a signature is released) to show what the code looks like and what goes wrong when state is mishandled. It is not SLH-DSA and is not interoperable. It then estimates the hash-call cost per signature for four FIPS 205 sets from the structure; these estimates are my own derivation and not taken from the standard. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

import hashlib, math

# A toy stateful hash-based signature (WOTS chains plus a Merkle tree of 16 keys). It is NOT SLH-DSA: it only shows how such code is structured.
counter = {"hash": 0}
def H(data):
    counter["hash"] += 1
    return hashlib.sha256(data).digest()
W, LEN1, LEN2 = 16, 64, 3                                              # 4 bits per digit: 64 message digits and 3 checksum digits
def chain(x, start, steps, tag):
    for i in range(start, start + steps):
        x = H(tag + bytes([i]) + x)
    return x
def digits(msg_digest):
    ds = [v for byte in msg_digest for v in (byte >> 4, byte & 15)]
    checksum = sum(W - 1 - d for d in ds)
    return ds + [(checksum >> 8) & 15, (checksum >> 4) & 15, checksum & 15]
def wots_secret(seed, leaf, i):
    return hashlib.sha256(seed + leaf.to_bytes(4, "big") + bytes([i])).digest()
def wots_public(seed, leaf):
    tops = [chain(wots_secret(seed, leaf, i), 0, W - 1, bytes([i])) for i in range(LEN1 + LEN2)]
    return H(b"".join(tops))
def wots_sign(seed, leaf, msg_digest):
    return [chain(wots_secret(seed, leaf, i), 0, d, bytes([i])) for i, d in enumerate(digits(msg_digest))]
def wots_public_from_sig(sig, msg_digest):
    tops = [chain(s, d, W - 1 - d, bytes([i])) for i, (s, d) in enumerate(zip(sig, digits(msg_digest)))]
    return H(b"".join(tops))

HEIGHT = 4
class StatefulSigner:
    def __init__(self, seed):
        self.seed, self.next_leaf = seed, 0
        leaves = [wots_public(seed, i) for i in range(2 ** HEIGHT)]
        self.levels = [leaves]
        while len(self.levels[-1]) > 1:
            lv = self.levels[-1]
            self.levels.append([H(lv[i] + lv[i + 1]) for i in range(0, len(lv), 2)])
        self.public_key = self.levels[-1][0]
    def sign(self, message):
        leaf = self.next_leaf
        if leaf >= 2 ** HEIGHT:
            raise RuntimeError("all one-time keys used")
        self.next_leaf += 1                                              # the state MUST be persisted before the signature is released
        digest = hashlib.sha256(message).digest()
        path, idx = [], leaf
        for lv in self.levels[:-1]:
            path.append(lv[idx ^ 1]); idx //= 2
        return leaf, wots_sign(self.seed, leaf, digest), path
def verify(public_key, message, signature):
    leaf, sig, path = signature
    node = wots_public_from_sig(sig, hashlib.sha256(message).digest())
    for sibling in path:
        node = H(node + sibling) if leaf % 2 == 0 else H(sibling + node)
        leaf //= 2
    return node == public_key

seed = b"toy seed for the lesson".ljust(32, b"\0")
signer = StatefulSigner(seed)
print("signer built; one-time keys available:", 2 ** HEIGHT)
sig = signer.sign(b"image-1")
counter["hash"] = 0
ok = verify(signer.public_key, b"image-1", sig)
print("signature verifies:", ok, "| hash calls to verify:", counter["hash"], "| wrong message rejected:", not verify(signer.public_key, b"image-2", sig))
print("signature content: leaf index + 67 chain values + 4 tree siblings =", 67 + 4, "hash-sized values of 32 bytes =", (67 + 4) * 32, "bytes")
s2, s3 = signer.sign(b"image-2"), signer.sign(b"image-3")
print("leaf indices handed out:", sig[0], s2[0], s3[0], "| all valid:", all(verify(signer.public_key, m, s) for m, s in ((b"image-1", sig), (b"image-2", s2), (b"image-3", s3))))
restored = StatefulSigner(seed)                                          # a restored backup that forgot the counter
dup = restored.sign(b"transfer 1 coin")
da, db = digits(hashlib.sha256(b"image-1").digest()), digits(hashlib.sha256(b"transfer 1 coin").digest())
print("a restored backup reuses leaf", dup[0], "already used for image-1; the two digests differ in", sum(x != y for x, y in zip(da, db)), "of 67 digit positions, and at each the attacker now holds chain values at two depths (see 8.7)")

print()
print("estimated hash calls per signature for four FIPS 205 sets (derived here from the structure, not read from the standard; w = 16):")
print(f"{'set':<6} {'sign':>12} {'verify (average)':>18}")
for name, n, h, d, hp, a, k in (("128s", 16, 63, 7, 9, 12, 14), ("128f", 16, 66, 22, 3, 6, 33), ("192s", 24, 63, 7, 9, 14, 17), ("256s", 32, 64, 8, 8, 14, 22)):
    len1 = -(-8 * n // 4)
    ln = len1 + int(math.log2(len1 * 15) / 4) + 1
    sign = d * (2 ** hp) * (ln * 15 + 1) + k * (2 ** a) * 2              # rebuild the used XMSS trees and the FORS leaves
    verify_calls = k * (a + 1) + d * (ln * 7.5 + hp + 1)
    print(f"{name:<6} {sign:>12,} {verify_calls:>18,.0f}")

blocks.markdown:
The toy signature has 71 hash-sized values, 2,272 bytes (67 chain values plus 4 tree siblings), verifies after 560 hash calls, and detects a modified message. The state counter hands out leaf indices 0, 1, 2 and each signature verifies. The failure the code illustrates is the operational one: a **restored backup** that forgot the counter signs a new message with leaf 0 again, and because the two digests differ in 65 of 67 digit positions, an attacker holding both signatures has chain values at two depths at almost every position and can forge (lesson 8.7 showed the same effect for Lamport keys). Stateful standards (XMSS, LMS) therefore require the state to be persisted *before* a signature is released and forbid cloning the signer; SLH-DSA's design removes this requirement, at the price of far larger signatures.

The estimates show the cost shape of SLH-DSA: roughly 2 to 3.3 million hash calls to sign for the small "s" sets against about 100,000 for 128f, and only about 2,000 to 6,000 to verify. So signing is the bottleneck, and the "f" (fast) sets trade larger signatures (17,088 against 7,856 bytes for the 128-bit sets) for a much cheaper signature generation. **Common mistakes** in real code: copying or snapshotting the signer state, signing from two processes with the same key, and treating signing time as uniform when it is dominated by tree recomputation.

sections.title: 9.4 Key Generation (Engineering Depth)
sections.summary: Seed handling and per-purpose derivation with HKDF, the FIPS 203 key checks, and a measurement of which kinds of key corruption each check actually detects.

blocks.markdown:
Key generation is where an implementation meets the quality of its randomness (see 7.10 and C10). FIPS 203 requires the two 32-byte random strings to come from an **approved random bit generator** (SP 800-90A/B/C), generated freshly for every call; a seed must never be reused or shared between algorithms. When one master secret is held (for example in a hardware module or a key-management service), distinct **labelled derivations** (HKDF with a purpose string) give independent seeds for each algorithm, version and use.

The standard also describes optional **checks on a key pair received from another source** (section 7.1): a seed-consistency check (regenerate from the seed), an encapsulation-key check, a decapsulation-key check, and a **pair-wise consistency test** that encapsulates and decapsulates and compares. The decapsulation-key check (section 7.3) is a type check and a hash check: H of the embedded ek must equal the stored hash. The standard itself notes that these checks do not guarantee that a key was properly generated. The listing derives seeds with HKDF, shows the library rejecting seeds of the wrong length, and then measures **what each check catches** by flipping one bit in each region of a decapsulation key. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_768
from dilithium_py.ml_dsa import ML_DSA_65

# --- one master secret, independent per-purpose seeds (HKDF with distinct labels), so no seed is ever shared between algorithms
master = bytes(range(32, 64))                                              # a fixed value for the lesson; in practice it comes from an approved random generator
def derive(label, length):
    return HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=length, salt=None, info=label).derive(master)
kem_seed, dsa_seed = derive(b"ml-kem-768 key seed v1", 64), derive(b"ml-dsa-65 key seed v1", 32)
print("seeds differ and have the right lengths:", kem_seed != dsa_seed[:32] + dsa_seed, len(kem_seed), len(dsa_seed))
ek, dk = ML_KEM_768.key_derive(kem_seed)
print("the same master secret and label always give the same key pair:", (ek, dk) == ML_KEM_768.key_derive(derive(b"ml-kem-768 key seed v1", 64)), "| a different label gives a different one:", ek != ML_KEM_768.key_derive(derive(b"ml-kem-768 key seed v2", 64))[0])
for bad in (b"", bytes(32), bytes(63), bytes(65)):
    try:
        ML_KEM_768.key_derive(bad)
        print(f"seed of {len(bad)} bytes accepted")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"seed of {len(bad)} bytes rejected: {type(exc).__name__}")

# --- key checks of FIPS 203 section 7.3: type check and hash check of the decapsulation key, then pair-wise consistency

sections.title: 9.5 Encapsulation/Decapsulation
sections.summary: The encapsulation-key modulus check implemented and tested, implicit rejection verified against SHAKE256(z || c), and input length checks.

blocks.markdown:
Encapsulation must be run only on a **checked** encapsulation key (FIPS 203, section 7.2). The check has two parts: a **type check** (the key is a byte array of exactly 384·k + 32 bytes) and a **modulus check** (ByteEncode12(ByteDecode12(ek[0:384k])) must equal ek[0:384k]); because ByteDecode12 reduces each 12-bit value modulo q = 3329, the round trip changes the bytes whenever a coefficient is 3329 or larger. The check need not be performed on every call, but assurance that it has been done is required. Decapsulation has its own input checks (the ciphertext length and the dk hash check) and then the **implicit rejection** of the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform (7.6): it re-encrypts the decrypted message, and if the result differs from the received ciphertext it does **not** signal an error but returns the pseudo-random key K̄ = J(z ‖ c), with J = SHAKE256 and z the secret value stored in dk. An attacker who submits modified ciphertexts therefore gets no signal about validity.

The listing implements the modulus check from the standard and tests honest, truncated and out-of-range keys; it then tests implicit rejection: a tampered ciphertext does not raise an error, the returned key equals SHAKE256(z ‖ c) exactly as the standard specifies, and 136 sampled single-bit flips all changed the key. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

import hashlib
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_768

kem = ML_KEM_768

seed = bytes(range(64))

z = dk[-32:]

# --- encapsulation key check of FIPS 203 section 7.2: type check, then modulus check ByteEncode12(ByteDecode12(ek[0:384k])) == ek[0:384k]
def byte_decode12(data):
    bits = int.from_bytes(data, "little")
    return [((bits >> (12 * i)) & 0xFFF) % 3329 for i in range(len(data) * 8 // 12)]          # ByteDecode12 reduces modulo q
def byte_encode12(values):
    bits = 0
    for i, v in enumerate(values):
        bits |= (v & 0xFFF) << (12 * i)
    return bits.to_bytes(len(values) * 12 // 8, "little")
def ek_check(candidate):
    if len(candidate) != 384 * k + 32:
        return "type check failed"
    body = candidate[:384 * k]
    if byte_encode12(byte_decode12(body)) != body:
        return "modulus check failed"
    return "ok"
print("honest ek:", ek_check(ek))
too_short = ek[:-1]
print("ek one byte short:", ek_check(too_short))
bad_coeff = bytearray(ek)
bad_coeff[0:2] = (4000 | (int.from_bytes(bad_coeff[0:2], "little") & 0xF000)).to_bytes(2, "little")           # first coefficient 4000 >= q = 3329

print("why the round trip catches it: decoding reduces 4000 modulo q to", 4000 % 3329, "and re-encoding therefore differs from the received bytes")
try:
    kem.encaps(bytes(bad_coeff))
    print("this library's encaps accepted the out-of-range key (the caller must run the check)")
except Exception as exc:
    print("this library's encaps rejects it itself:", type(exc).__name__)

# --- implicit rejection: a tampered ciphertext yields a pseudo-random key derived from the secret value z, never an error

print()
print("honest decapsulation matches:", kem.decaps(dk, ct) == key)

expected = hashlib.shake_256(z + bytes(tampered)).digest(32)               # K_bar = J(z || c)
print("tampered ciphertext: no exception, a different key:", rejected_key != key, "| equals SHAKE256(z || c) as in FIPS 203:", rejected_key == expected)

changed = sum(kem.decaps(dk, ct[:i] + bytes([ct[i] ^ 1]) + ct[i + 1:]) != key for i in range(0, len(ct), len(ct) // trials + 1))

for bad_ct in (ct[:-1], ct + b"\x00", b""):
    try:

        print(f"ciphertext of {len(bad_ct)} bytes accepted")
    except Exception as exc:
        print(f"ciphertext of {len(bad_ct)} bytes rejected before decryption (type check): {type(exc).__name__}")

sections.title: 9.6 Signing/Verification
sections.summary: Which malformed signatures a verifier must reject and how: truncation, wrong length, hint abuse, corrupted components, tested one by one.

blocks.markdown:
A signature verifier is a parser of attacker-controlled bytes, so its first job is **strict input validation**: the length must be exactly the fixed size for the parameter set, the components must decode, the hint vector must be well formed (at most ω non-zero entries, indices in strictly increasing order within each polynomial, padding bytes zero), and the response vector z must satisfy the norm bound. Only then is the algebraic check performed. Accepting any non-canonical encoding of a valid signature would also break **strong unforgeability**: an attacker could produce a second, different byte string that verifies for the same message.

An ML-DSA-44 signature is c̃ (32 bytes) ‖ z (4 polynomials × 32 × 18 bytes = 2,304) ‖ hint (ω + k = 84 bytes), 2,420 bytes in total (FIPS 204, Table 2). The listing builds nine malformed variants (truncation, extra byte, empty, all zero, flipped challenge bit, flipped z bit, hint region zeroed, hint counts larger than ω, indices out of order) and also corrupts a valid signature at random 300 times, and records what the verifier does. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

import random
from dilithium_py.ml_dsa import ML_DSA_44

dsa = ML_DSA_44
pk, sk = dsa.key_derive(bytes(range(32)))
m = b"configuration bundle 42"
sig = dsa.sign(sk, m)

print("layout: c_tilde", c_len, "| z", z_len, "| hint", h_len, "| total", c_len + z_len + h_len, "=", len(sig))

def outcome(candidate):
    try:
        return "accepted" if dsa.verify(pk, m, candidate) else "rejected"
    except Exception as exc:
        return f"raised {type(exc).__name__}"

cases = {

    "one byte appended": sig + b"\x00",

for name, candidate in cases.items():
    print(f"{name:<46} {outcome(candidate)}")

sections.title: 9.7 Serialization
sections.summary: ByteEncode and ByteDecode from FIPS 203 implemented, checked against kyber-py's key bytes, and the exact error of compression measured over all inputs.

blocks.markdown:
Interoperability depends on **byte-exact encodings**. FIPS 203 packs a polynomial of 256 coefficients into 32·d bytes with ByteEncode_d (d bits per coefficient, little endian, section 4.2.1); keys use d = 12 (384 bytes per polynomial), and ciphertexts first **compress** coefficients to d_u or d_v bits, a lossy rounding that saves bandwidth. Compress_d(x) = ⌈(2^d/q)·x⌋ mod 2^d and Decompress_d(y) = ⌈(q/2^d)·y⌋, and decompressing a compressed value returns a number whose distance from the original is at most ⌈q/2^(d+1)⌋; that error is part of the noise budget and is included in the failure analysis of FIPS 203 Table 1.

The listing implements ByteEncode and ByteDecode (with the modular reduction of ByteDecode12), checks the round trip for six values of d, re-encodes the coefficients of a real kyber-py encapsulation key and compares the bytes, and then measures the compression error **exhaustively over all 3,329 inputs** for each d used by the standard. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

import random
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_768

q = 3329
def byte_encode(values, d):                                             # FIPS 203, Algorithm 5: d bits per coefficient, little endian
    bits = 0
    for i, v in enumerate(values):
        bits |= v << (d * i)
    return bits.to_bytes(len(values) * d // 8, "little")
def byte_decode(data, d):                                               # FIPS 203, Algorithm 6
    bits = int.from_bytes(data, "little")
    m = 2 ** d if d < 12 else q
    return [((bits >> (d * i)) & (2 ** d - 1)) % m for i in range(len(data) * 8 // d)]
def compress(x, d):                                                     # round(2^d / q * x) mod 2^d, in exact integer arithmetic
    return ((x << d) + q // 2) // q % (2 ** d)
def decompress(y, d):                                                   # round(q / 2^d * y)
    return ((y * q) + (1 << (d - 1))) >> d

rng = random.Random(3)
for d in (1, 4, 5, 10, 11, 12):
    values = [rng.randrange(2 ** d if d < 12 else q) for _ in range(256)]
    encoded = byte_encode(values, d)
    assert len(encoded) == 32 * d and byte_decode(encoded, d) == values
print("ByteEncode_d / ByteDecode_d round trip for d in {1, 4, 5, 10, 11, 12}: 256 coefficients occupy 32 * d bytes (384 bytes for d = 12)")

ek, dk = ML_KEM_768.key_derive(bytes(range(64)))
body = ek[:384 * ML_KEM_768.k]
coefficients = byte_decode(body, 12)
print("kyber-py's encapsulation key re-encodes to the same bytes with my encoder:", byte_encode(coefficients, 12) == body, f"| {len(coefficients)} coefficients, all below q: {all(c < q for c in coefficients)}")
print("last 32 bytes of ek are the matrix seed rho; their share of the key is", f"{32 / len(ek):.1%}")

print()

for d in (1, 4, 5, 10, 11):
    bound = (q + (1 << d)) // (1 << (d + 1))
    worst = max(min((x - decompress(compress(x, d), d)) % q, (decompress(compress(x, d), d) - x) % q) for x in range(q))
    print(f"{d:>3} {bound:>25} {worst:>36} {str(worst <= bound):>13}")
print("compression to d bits is lossy: the error it adds is part of the noise budget (ciphertext uses d_u = 10 and d_v = 4 for ML-KEM-768)")

print("size from the encodings: ek =", sizes["ek"], "bytes, ciphertext =", sizes["ciphertext"], "bytes (FIPS 203 Table 3: 1184 and 1088)")

sections.title: 9.8 API Design
sections.summary: A small API that is hard to misuse, built and attacked: bound algorithm names, size checks, a single error, wipeable secrets and no exposed internals.

blocks.markdown:
Most cryptographic failures in deployed systems are **API misuse**, not broken algorithms. A good KEM or signature API makes the safe path the easy path: keys are **opaque objects** with the algorithm identifier built in, so a ciphertext for ML-KEM-512 cannot silently be fed to an ML-KEM-768 key; **randomness is generated inside** the module (FIPS 203 section 3.3); the deterministic internals are not exported; sizes and types are checked at the boundary; a failed decapsulation returns the **implicit-rejection key and no error detail**; secrets live in objects that can be wiped, have no readable representation, and are compared with constant-time functions; and a destroyed key cannot be used again.

The listing implements a tiny wrapper around kyber-py with these properties and then attacks it with the usual misuse cases: a ciphertext for another parameter set, a truncated ciphertext, an unknown algorithm name, a malformed public key, a tampered ciphertext and use after destroy. Every refusal uses a single error type with no information about the reason, except where the caller's own mistake is obvious (wrong algorithm name). The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

Each misuse case ended in the same controlled way: a `KemError` with a short message, and the tampered ciphertext produced a different key without any error, as implicit rejection requires. The design rules are visible in a few lines of code, and they are cheap compared with the cost of the failure they prevent. Two points deserve emphasis. sections.title: 9.9 Memory Considerations
sections.summary: Sizes of keys, ciphertexts and working objects computed from the parameters, the memory/time tradeoff for the public matrix, and what wiping secrets can and cannot do in Python.

blocks.markdown:
Memory matters twice: **how much** an implementation needs (important on embedded devices and in protocol buffers) and **how long secrets stay** in it. The persistent objects are fixed by the standards: ML-KEM-768 has a 1,184-byte encapsulation key, a 2,400-byte decapsulation key and a 1,088-byte ciphertext; ML-DSA-65 has a 1,952-byte public key, a 4,032-byte private key and a 3,309-byte signature (FIPS 203 Table 3, FIPS 204 Table 2). During the computation the largest object is the public matrix: k × k polynomials, 512 bytes each when stored as 16-bit coefficients, so 2,048 bytes for k = 2 and 8,192 bytes for k = 4. Implementations on small devices avoid storing it by **regenerating each polynomial from the 32-byte seed ρ** every time it is needed, which saves memory and costs extra hashing: a classic time-versus-memory trade-off.

The second concern is **secret lifetime**. Secret material should be wiped as soon as it is no longer needed, kept out of logs, crash dumps, swap files and memory pages shared with other processes. In languages with managed memory, the language can undermine this: immutable objects cannot be wiped, copies are made freely, and the garbage collector decides when memory is reused. The listing computes the sizes from the parameters and then demonstrates concretely what Python allows. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

The tables reproduce the standard sizes and show the structure of the working memory: a single polynomial is 512 bytes, a vector of k polynomials 1 to 2 KB, and the matrix grows with k² to 8 KB for ML-KEM-1024. For ML-DSA the polynomials are wider (int32), and signing keeps several vectors alive (the table's column is a rough estimate of three such vectors, not a measured figure) while the rejection loop repeats. The wiping demonstration shows the limit in a managed language: a `bytearray` can be zeroed in place and every view of it sees the change, but any earlier `bytes(...)` copy is a separate immutable object that remains in memory, and a `bytes` object cannot be wiped at all. This is the reason serious implementations of key handling are written in languages that give explicit control (C with `explicit_bzero`/`memset_s`, Rust with the `zeroize` crate) and why Python code should keep keys in wipeable buffers, avoid converting them to `bytes`, and rely on the operating system or a hardware module for real protection.

**Common mistakes:** assuming that `del key` or setting a variable to `None` erases anything, leaving keys in exception tracebacks and debug logs, and allowing secrets into core dumps or swap (lock the memory pages and disable dumps for key-holding processes).

sections.title: 9.10 Performance
sections.summary: Where the arithmetic goes in ML-KEM (operation counts from the NTT of lesson 8.3), and measured timings of pure Python against OpenSSL.

blocks.markdown:
Performance claims need a method. The honest starting point is **operation counting**: in ML-KEM almost all arithmetic is polynomial multiplication done with the NTT, and the NTT costs a fixed number of modular multiplications (lesson 8.3: 896 for a forward transform, 1,152 for the inverse including the final scaling, 640 for a pointwise product of two transformed polynomials). Key generation transforms s and e and multiplies the matrix by s; encapsulation transforms y, multiplies by Aᵀ and by t, and applies inverse transforms; decapsulation decrypts and then **re-encrypts** to run the validity check. The first listing counts the multiplications for the three parameter sets. Hashing (SHA-3 for expanding the matrix and sampling noise) is not counted here, although in optimised code it often dominates.

Counts do not tell the time. The second listing measures wall-clock time of the pure-Python reference code against OpenSSL, but it is **not run in the build check**, because timings depend on the machine and on what else is running; the output shown is a sample from one run on the author's computer. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

NTT, INTT, POINTWISE = 896, 1152, 640        # modular multiplications for one forward NTT, one inverse NTT and one pointwise product (measured in lesson 8.3)

def keygen_muls(k):
    return 2 * k * NTT + k * k * POINTWISE                                  # NTT of s and e, then A o s

def decrypt_muls(k):
    return k * NTT + k * POINTWISE + INTT                                   # NTT of u, s o u, one inverse NTT

def encrypt_muls(k):
    return k * NTT + k * k * POINTWISE + k * INTT + k * POINTWISE + INTT    # NTT of y, A^T o y, k inverse NTTs, t o y, one more inverse NTT

sections.title: 9.11 Interoperability
sections.summary: Differential testing of two independent implementations (pure Python and OpenSSL): same keys from a seed, cross encapsulation and signing, identical rejection keys and identical verdicts on mutated signatures.

blocks.markdown:
Two correct implementations of a standard must produce **byte-identical results** for the same inputs, and must agree on which inputs are invalid. The strongest practical test is **differential testing**: run independent implementations side by side on many inputs, including malformed ones, and compare. This lab has two: the pure-Python reference libraries and OpenSSL, accessed through the `cryptography` package. For ML-KEM the interoperability points are: the same seed gives the same public key; a ciphertext produced by one implementation is decapsulated to the same shared secret by the other; and, because implicit rejection is deterministic, even the **pseudo-random key returned for a tampered ciphertext is identical** in both. For ML-DSA the points are: the same seed gives the same public key; signatures from either implementation verify in the other; and, for mutated signatures, both implementations reach the same accept/reject verdict.

Known-answer tests from a standards body would add reference values, but none were available in the lab; independent implementations are the next best evidence. The listing runs the comparisons on ML-KEM-768 and -1024 (the parameter sets available in this version of the OpenSSL interface) and on all three ML-DSA sets. The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

blocks.markdown:
All comparisons agree: the same keys result from a seed in every trial, ciphertexts and signatures cross-verify in both directions for all parameter sets tested, tampered ML-KEM ciphertexts give the same rejection key in both implementations (20 of 20 for each set), and of 600 randomly mutated ML-DSA signatures (200 per parameter set) both implementations returned the same verdict every time. That the rejection key matches is a strong signal: it depends on z and the whole ciphertext through SHAKE256 and is only identical if both implementations follow the same specification down to this corner of the decapsulation algorithm.

**What this does and does not show.** It shows that two independent implementations interoperate on these inputs, which is exactly what protocol deployments need. It does not prove either implementation correct on all inputs (a bug present in both, or one on inputs not generated here, would remain), it does not test the ML-KEM-512 set (not offered by this OpenSSL interface), and it says nothing about side-channel behaviour. **Practice:** keep an independent implementation in the test suite, regenerate the comparisons in CI on every library update, add the official known-answer vectors when available, and include malformed inputs.

sections.title: 9.12 Deployment Testing
sections.summary: A deployment gate that runs known-answer fingerprints, many random round trips with cross-checks, negative tests, a randomness smoke test and a fault test, and states what it does not prove.

blocks.markdown:
Before a post-quantum component ships, it needs a **repeatable gate** that answers one question: does this build behave exactly like the one that passed review? A practical gate has five layers. (1) **Known-answer tests**: derive everything from fixed seeds and compare a fingerprint of the outputs with a value pinned in the repository, so any change in any byte is caught. (2) **Round trips on many random keys**, cross-checked with an independent implementation. (3) **Negative tests**: wrong lengths, tampered ciphertexts and corrupted keys must be rejected or handled by implicit rejection, and must never crash. (4) A **randomness smoke test** (bit balance, no repeated shared secrets). It cannot certify a generator, but it catches a stuck or broken one. (5) A **fault test**: a corrupted stored key must not silently produce plausible output.

The listing runs these layers against ML-KEM-768 and prints a PASS/FAIL line for each check, and a final decision. A gate like this is cheap enough to run on every commit. It verifies *behaviour*; it cannot establish constant-time execution, memory safety or resistance to side channels, which need different tools (C10 and C11). The labs use the pure-Python reference libraries kyber-py (ML-KEM) and dilithium-py (ML-DSA), and `cryptography` 50.0.1 (OpenSSL) as an independent implementation. Everything runs on your own machine on keys generated in the lesson. The code teaches how implementations are structured and tested; it is reference code, slow and not hardened against side channels, and must not protect real data.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, json, random
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import mlkem
from kyber_py.ml_kem import ML_KEM_768

kem = ML_KEM_768
rng = random.Random(2026)
results = []
def gate(name, ok, detail=""):
    results.append((name, bool(ok)))
    print(f"[{'PASS' if ok else 'FAIL'}] {name}" + (f"  ({detail})" if detail else ""))

# 1. known-answer regression: derive everything from fixed seeds and fingerprint the outputs; a change in any byte changes the fingerprint
def fingerprint():
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    for i in range(10):
        seed = hashlib.shake_256(b"kat-seed-%d" % i).digest(64)
        ek, dk = kem.key_derive(seed)
        m = hashlib.shake_256(b"kat-msg-%d" % i).digest(32)
        key, ct = kem._encaps_internal(ek, m)                           # the deterministic internal function exists for testing only
        h.update(ek + dk + ct + key)
    return h.hexdigest()
first, second = fingerprint(), fingerprint()
gate("known-answer fingerprint is reproducible", first == second, f"sha256 {first[:16]}...")
pinned = first                                                          # in a real project this value is stored in the repository and compared in CI

# 2. functional round trips on many random keys, cross-checked against the independent OpenSSL implementation
ok_rt = ok_x = 0
for _ in range(60):
    seed = bytes(rng.getrandbits(8) for _ in range(64))
    ek, dk = kem.key_derive(seed)
    key, ct = kem.encaps(ek)
    ok_rt += kem.decaps(dk, ct) == key
    ok_x += mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey.from_seed_bytes(seed).decapsulate(ct) == key
gate("60 random round trips", ok_rt == 60)
gate("60 round trips cross-checked with OpenSSL", ok_x == 60)

# 3. negative tests: malformed and tampered inputs must be rejected or handled by implicit rejection, and never crash
ek, dk = kem.keygen()
key, ct = kem.encaps(ek)
def raises(fn):
    try:
        fn(); return False
    except ValueError:
        return True
gate("wrong-length ek rejected", raises(lambda: kem.encaps(ek[:-1])))
gate("wrong-length ciphertext rejected", raises(lambda: kem.decaps(dk, ct[:-1])))
gate("wrong-length dk rejected", raises(lambda: kem.decaps(dk[:-1], ct)))
flips = sum(kem.decaps(dk, ct[:i] + bytes([ct[i] ^ (1 << (i % 8))]) + ct[i + 1:]) != key for i in range(0, len(ct), 17))
gate("every sampled single-bit ciphertext flip changes the key (implicit rejection)", flips == len(range(0, len(ct), 17)), f"{flips} of {len(range(0, len(ct), 17))}")

# 4. randomness sanity: shared secrets from independent runs look uniform (a smoke test, not a certification)
secrets_ = b"".join(kem.encaps(ek)[0] for _ in range(300))
ones = sum(bin(byte).count("1") for byte in secrets_)
fraction = ones / (8 * len(secrets_))
gate("bit balance of 300 shared secrets within 1 percent of one half", abs(fraction - 0.5) < 0.01)
gate("no repeated shared secret in 300 runs", len({kem.encaps(ek)[0] for _ in range(300)}) == 300)

# 5. state and fault handling: a corrupted private key must not silently produce plausible output
bad_dk = bytearray(dk); bad_dk[10] ^= 1
gate("corrupted dk detected by a pair-wise test", kem.decaps(bytes(bad_dk), ct) != key)

failed = [name for name, ok in results if not ok]
print()
print(f"deployment gate: {len(results) - len(failed)} of {len(results)} checks passed", "-> release blocked: " + ", ".join(failed) if failed else "-> all checks passed")
print("this gate verifies behaviour only; it does not establish constant-time execution, memory safety or side-channel resistance (see C10 and C11)")

blocks.caption: Expected output

blocks.markdown:
All ten checks pass; the fingerprint of the known-answer run is reproducible between runs, 60 random round trips agree with each other and with OpenSSL, malformed lengths are rejected, all 64 sampled ciphertext bit flips change the returned key (implicit rejection), and the corrupted private key does not produce the honest shared secret. The value of the gate is in what it blocks: a regression in encoding, a changed constant, an accidental change of the sampling function, or a library update that changes behaviour will change the fingerprint or fail a cross-check, and the release stops with a named failing check.

**Limits, stated plainly.** A passing gate is not a security proof. The tests above do not detect timing or cache leaks, do not examine memory after use, do not show that the random generator is of cryptographic quality, and do not cover hardware faults beyond the single corruption tested. Production deployments add the official validation vectors, a code review of the constant-time properties, compiler and platform matrices, fuzzing of every parser, and, where required, certification of the module under the relevant validation programme.

blocks.question: What does a pinned known-answer fingerprint detect?
options: Any change in the outputs of a deterministic run, even in a single byte
blocks.explanation: The fingerprint hashes keys, ciphertexts and shared secrets from fixed seeds.

blocks.question: Which of these can a behavioural test gate NOT establish?
blocks.explanation: Those properties need timing analysis and code review (C10, C11).

blocks.question: Why cross-check round trips with an independent implementation?
options: A shared misunderstanding is unlikely to appear in two separate codebases
blocks.explanation: Agreement between independent implementations is stronger evidence than self-consistency.
